title: India and Canada Just Launched a Trade Forum. The Real Prize Is a Free Trade Deal by December.
excerpt: Piyush Goyal and Mark Carney are fast-tracking CEPA negotiations that could unlock a $50 billion trade corridor and reshape economic ties for 2.8 million Indian-Canadians.
body:
India and Canada have launched a new bilateral trade and investment forum, the most tangible outcome yet of a diplomatic reset that would have been unthinkable eighteen months ago.

The Canada-India Trade and Investment Forum was announced during Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal's three-day visit to Ottawa, where he held a series of meetings with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and senior cabinet ministers. In a joint statement, Goyal and Canadian Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu committed to concluding negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement by the end of 2026 — a timeline that both governments described as aggressive but achievable.

## From Diplomatic Crisis to Trade Corridor

The speed of the turnaround is striking. In late 2023 and through much of 2024, India-Canada relations were at their lowest point in decades, damaged by allegations linked to the killing of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia. Diplomats were expelled. Intelligence-sharing was frozen. Trade talks were shelved indefinitely.

The thaw began in mid-2025, accelerated when Carney — a former Bank of England and Bank of Canada governor — became prime minister and visited India in March 2026. CEPA negotiations were formally launched during that visit. A Canadian delegation came to New Delhi in May for the second round. Goyal's Ottawa trip marks the third round, with both sides issuing what officials described as "direct mandates" to their negotiating teams.

Carney framed the agreement in pragmatic terms: "This will be a game changer for Canadian workers and businesses — unlocking a massive new market."

## The Stakes Are Large

Both governments have set a target of $50 billion in bilateral trade by 2030. Current trade sits at approximately $12 billion, meaning the agreement would need to catalyse a fourfold increase in four years.

The sectors identified for cooperation suggest where the growth is expected: clean energy, critical minerals, agri-food, advanced manufacturing, digital technologies, and skills development. Canada sits on some of the world's largest deposits of lithium, nickel, cobalt, and potash — minerals India desperately needs for its electric vehicle ambitions and agricultural productivity. India offers a consumer market of 1.4 billion people, a deep bench of STEM talent, and a manufacturing base scaling rapidly under production-linked incentive schemes.

The India-Oman CEPA, which entered into force on June 1, offers a template. That agreement grants duty-free access to nearly 98 percent of Indian exports. If the India-Canada CEPA follows a similar structure, it could transform market access for Indian exporters in textiles, gems and jewellery, food processing, and IT services.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the 2.8 million people of Indian origin living in Canada — 1.8 million Indo-Canadians and roughly one million NRIs including students — the trade agreement carries weight beyond tariff schedules.

The joint statement emphasised improving "people-to-people ties, business mobility, and direct commercial linkages." In practical terms, that means smoother movement for professionals, entrepreneurs, and students between the two countries. It also means that the political relationship underpinning their daily lives — the diplomatic architecture that determines visa processing times, consular access, and the tone of public discourse — is on firmer ground.

Sidhu confirmed that Canada will lead a "Team Canada Trade Mission" to India later this year, an unusual step that signals the depth of business interest. During Goyal's meetings with Canadian corporate leaders, discussions covered insurance, food processing, banking, critical minerals, and Global Capability Centres.

## A Wider Strategy

The India-Canada forum is part of a broader Indian trade offensive. India has signed nine free trade agreements in the past three and a half years, covering 38 developed economies. Six to seven more are expected to enter force in the next year, including a first-tranche deal with the United States that is nearing signature.

The pattern is clear: India is building a web of preferential trade relationships designed to reduce dependence on any single corridor and diversify supply chains away from China. Canada, with its resource wealth, technology sector, and large Indian diaspora, fits neatly into that architecture.

Whether the December deadline for CEPA is met depends on the details — agricultural tariffs, dairy access, and intellectual property provisions have historically been sticking points in Indian trade negotiations. But the political will is unmistakable, and for both countries, the cost of another diplomatic rupture is now visibly higher than the cost of compromise.
